findings.issue_text: [BUG] The call site installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source) passes two positional arguments, but integration subclasses that override should_sync with the old single-argument signature raise TypeError at runtime. Any integration (e.g. Jira, GitHub) defining `def should_sync(self, attribute)` without the new second parameter crashes with `TypeError: should_sync() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given` when the sync_assignee_outbound task invokes it, turning every assignment sync for that integration into a failed task instead of a sync decision.

[BUG] The task passes the new keyword `assignment_source=` to installation.sync_assignee_outbound, but the diff updates the abstract signature for sync_status_outbound only and never adds assignment_source to the sync_assignee_outbound abstract method contract in the mixin. The call compiles only by accident: every integration's concrete sync_assignee_outbound must happen to accept **kwargs for the new keyword to be swallowed silently, and any override with an explicit parameter list (the contract the abstract method declares) raises TypeError on every outbound assignment; meanwhile the kwarg the mixin documents (sync_status_outbound) is never passed by this code path, so the anti-cycle plumbing is attached to the wrong method.

[BUG] The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates timezone.now() once at module import, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value carries the module-load timestamp, not the actual assignment time. All assignment events produced after process startup report the same import-time timestamp (dataclass defaults are not per-instance factories the way default_factory would be), corrupting any downstream use of queued for ordering or freshness; the field is also serialized into celery kwargs where it deserializes back as an ISO string, so AssignmentSource instances reconstructed via from_dict have queued as str, violating the declared datetime type.

[BUG] assignment_source.to_dict() embeds a datetime object into celery apply_async kwargs, and on deserialization from_dict feeds the resulting ISO string back into the dataclass constructor unvalidated, so the reconstructed AssignmentSource has queued as str instead of datetime. The round-trip through the broker silently changes the type of the queued field: any consumer that calls .isoformat() or compares queued to a datetime on the worker side raises AttributeError/TypeError; from_dict's except (ValueError, TypeError) does not catch this because a string is accepted as the field value.

[ADVISORY] The cycle-prevention comparison uses sync_source.integration_id against org_integration.integration_id without verifying these ids live in the same id-space (Integration.id vs OrganizationIntegration.integration_id foreign key), an assumption the diff never validates. If org_integration.integration_id is ever a different identifier class (e.g. after hybrid-cloud RPC reshaping where org_integration rows are region-side and integration ids are control-side), the equality silently never matches and sync cycles return, or falsely match and block legitimate cross-integration propagation; no test in the diff exercises the non-matching multi-integration case.

[ADVISORY] The test named test_from_dict_inalid_data asserts from_dict returns None for a dict with unknown keys, but the except clause catches TypeError from unexpected kwargs while a dict with correct keys but wrong value types (e.g. integration_id='abc') is accepted without error, so the test documents a validation guarantee from_dict does not actually provide. Future callers relying on from_dict as a validation boundary (per the test's name) will accept malformed payloads like {"source_name": 1, "integration_id": "not-an-int"} and produce a dataclass with garbage field values instead of None.

[BUG] The cycle-prevention mechanism only guards the assignee path; sync_status_outbound gained an assignment_source parameter that no caller passes and should_sync for status/status_inbound never receives a sync_source, so status resolve/unresolve cycles are still possible despite the PR's stated goal of preventing sync-cycles. A resolve in Jira propagates status to Sentry, which propagates back to Jira and to every other linked integration with no source check, producing unbounded status-sync loops that the assignee fix was specifically designed to stop.

[BUG] The dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource created in the process (including all from_integration calls) carries the same import-time timestamp instead of its actual creation time. Any consumer relying on `queued` to order or age-limit sync events reads a timestamp that is off by the process's entire uptime; test_to_dict's `assert result.get("queued") is not None` masks this because it never existed as None.

[BUG] Rolling-deploy skew: sync_group_assignee_outbound now always enqueues the new kwarg assignment_source_dict, but workers running the pre-deploy version of sync_assignee_outbound do not accept that parameter and will raise TypeError on every assignee-sync task until all workers are updated. During any rolling deploy, every outbound assignee sync fired by an already-updated web tier crashes on old Celery workers with an unexpected-keyword TypeError, silently dropping assignee propagation.

[BUG] from_dict performs no type validation: a dict whose integration_id arrives as a string (e.g. after JSON round-trip through a broker that coerces it, or a hand-crafted producer) constructs an AssignmentSource with integration_id="123", and the equality check in should_sync (sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id) silently evaluates False, bypassing cycle prevention rather than failing. Cycle suppression is silently disabled for malformed or type-drifted payloads instead of being rejected, reintroducing the exact sync-loop the feature exists to prevent with no error signal.

[BUG] The self-cycle check blocks only same-integration propagation, but the comment's stated safe behavior leaves a two-integration ping-pong unhandled: an inbound assign from Jira propagates outbound to a co-linked GitHub issue, whose inbound handler assigns with the GitHub source and propagates outbound back to Jira (source GitHub != Jira integration_id), so the assignee assignment bounces between integrations indefinitely. Organizations with one Sentry group linked to two sync-enabled integrations that both support inbound assignee sync enter an assign/unassign ping-pong loop across the two systems on every inbound assignment.

[ADVISORY] The `queued` field is ships-inert: nothing in the diff reads it, and no test exercises a from_dict(to_dict(x)) round-trip, which is the only path that actually crosses the Celery boundary. A regression in serialization round-tripping (e.g. queued coming back as an ISO string, which dataclasses silently accept) would go undetected; the next consumer of `queued` inherits a field whose default value is broken and whose round-trip behavior is unverified.

[ADVISORY] from_dict returning None on any ValueError/TypeError silently downgrades a source-tagged sync to an untagged one, re-enabling the self-cycle the producer explicitly tried to prevent, with no log line to diagnose it. When a payload fails to parse, the sync proceeds without cycle protection and the operator gets no signal that loop-prevention was skipped; a debug-level or warning log would make the failure visible.

[BUG] The dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource constructed after process start carries the same import-time timestamp, not the time the assignment was made. Any consumer that relies on `queued` to order or age assignment events gets a monotonically stale timestamp shared by all sources; the field records nothing meaningful about the actual assignment.

[BUG] AssignmentSource.from_dict returns None on any parse failure, and the task silently downgrades that to 'no source', which re-enables the outbound sync the cycle guard exists to prevent. A malformed, truncated, or legacy-shaped assignment_source_dict in the Celery kwargs causes the cycle-prevention invariant to be silently skipped, so an inbound assignment echoed back from the same integration re-triggers an outbound sync instead of being suppressed — the exact loop this PR is meant to stop, triggered nondeterministically on bad payloads rather than failing loudly.

[ADVISORY] The abstract sync_status_outbound signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter that no call site in this diff ever passes, and the status sync path has no cycle guard at all. Under-scoping relative to the PR's stated goal of cross-system sync-cycle prevention: status (resolve/unresolve) sync remains fully exposed to the same A<->B echo loop that assignment now guards against, while the dead parameter invites implementers to believe status cycles are handled. Staff reviewers will flag that the invariant is enforced for one attribute and merely decorated for the other.

[ADVISORY] The `queued` field and `source_name` field are never read anywhere in this diff — source_name is informational only and queued is consumed by nothing, yet both are serialized across the Celery boundary via to_dict. Ships-inert surface: every future change to the dataclass shape (renames, field additions) now has a cross-process serialization compatibility constraint (old workers receiving new-field dicts will hit from_dict's TypeError fallback and silently lose the cycle guard) without any present functionality depending on these fields. Deletion of `queued` (and the timezone import) passes the deletion test outright.

[ADVISORY] sync_group_assignee_inbound fabricates the AssignmentSource from the integration, but GroupAssignee.assign/deassign callers outside the inbound-sync path (UI assignment, autoassignment, other plugins) pass no source, so the cycle guard only holds on the inbound path that was manually updated. The invariant 'an integration's own inbound change is never echoed back to it' is enforced only where this diff remembered to thread the parameter; any assign() call site added later (or existing ones triggered by another integration's inbound flow that goes through GroupAssignee.objects.assign indirectly) silently re-enables echo loops. A default source derived at the model layer, or enforcement inside sync_assignee_outbound keyed on the recorded actor, would remove the per-call-site burden.

[ADVISORY] IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync's signature was widened to accept sync_source but the base implementation ignores it, while the cycle-guard semantics live only in the IssueSyncIntegration subclass — every other should_sync implementation and caller must now know whether to pass the parameter. Parallel-maintenance burden: callers that pass sync_source to a subclass overriding should_sync without the parameter (or subclass overrides that forget to accept it) break at call time; the contract 'should_sync may or may not honor the source' is not enforced anywhere. Consolidating the source check into the shared key/config lookup would remove the split.

[BUG] AssignmentSource.to_dict() embeds a datetime ('queued') into Celery task kwargs, which the JSON task serializer cannot encode, so every outbound assignee sync that carries a source (i.e., the entire inbound-triggered path) raises a serialization error instead of enqueueing. When an inbound integration assignment triggers sync_group_assignee_outbound with an assignment_source, apply_async fails to serialize kwargs['assignment_source_dict'] (datetime not JSON-serializable), the task never runs, and the external issue is never assigned — inbound syncs silently break in production.

[BUG] The dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource instance shares the same process-start timestamp rather than its actual creation time. The 'queued' field is meaningless — all sources created during the process lifetime carry the server's boot time; any consumer using it for ordering/diagnostics gets wrong data, and it also feeds the unserializable datetime into to_dict().

[BUG] from_dict returns None on any malformed payload, which silently disables the sync-cycle guard: a task with a corrupt/legacy assignment_source_dict parses to None and should_sync treats it as 'no source', re-propagating the assignment back to the integration that originated it. A single bad or truncated payload on the queue turns the cycle-prevention design into a no-op for that task, causing an inbound→outbound bounce loop between Sentry and the provider; the failure mode is silent (no log, no metric), which is the exact scenario the guard exists to prevent.

[ADVISORY] The cycle guard is wired only into the assignee path; should_sync calls for status/comment sync (and the sync_status_outbound abstract method that gained an assignment_source parameter) have no caller in this diff passing a sync_source, so inbound status changes still bounce back to the originating integration. The stated design goal ('prevent sync-cycles') is only half-implemented: a status change received inbound from integration X propagates outbound to integration X, duplicating the exact cycle this artifact exists to fix; the next author extending this to status sync must rediscover the wiring.

[ADVISORY] IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync signature changed to accept sync_source, but any subclass overriding the old one-arg signature (should_sync(self, attribute)) will raise TypeError when the task invokes it with the new keyword. Out-of-tree or in-repo integration subclasses that override should_sync with the old signature crash on every assignee sync task once this ships; this is an interface change whose implementers are not all visible/updated in the diff.

[ADVISORY] Passing the assignment source through the task queue as a raw untyped dict (assignment_source_dict) couples the wire format to the dataclass shape with no versioning — renaming a field or adding a required one makes from_dict return None and silently drops cycle protection for in-flight messages during a rolling deploy. During a rolling deploy, old workers receiving new-format dicts (or new workers receiving old producers' dicts missing a field) get None from from_dict and re-enable the sync loop; a small named-typed envelope with an explicit version, or passing integration_id directly, would eliminate the whole class.

[ADVISORY] The test class name 'TestAssignmentSource' and test 'test_from_dict_empty_array' are misnomers, and 'inalid' is a typo, signaling the serialization round-trip through the Celery broker — the riskiest part of this design — is never tested. The datetime-in-kwargs serialization failure (see sync.py finding) goes green in CI because to_dict()/from_dict() are only tested in-process with Python objects; a test that round-trips through the task serializer would have caught it.

[BUG] AssignmentSource uses `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a dataclass field default, which is evaluated once at module import, so every instance shares the process-start timestamp instead of the actual assignment time. Any consumer relying on `queued` to order or age assignment events gets a stale timestamp equal to worker/import time, not the assignment time; and it silently obscures real event time.

[BUG] `assignment_source.to_dict()` embeds a `datetime` (`queued`) into Celery `apply_async` kwargs, which the default JSON task serializer cannot serialize, causing enqueue to fail with a serialization error. Any code path that calls sync_group_assignee_outbound with a non-None assignment_source (e.g. the inbound unassign path at line 96-99) crashes the outbound sync enqueue instead of syncing the assignment to external systems — the assignment propagation is silently lost (or raises in the request path), a regression from the previous always-sync behavior.

[BUG] The cycle-prevention guard is applied only in the outbound-assignee should_sync path, while the stated intent ('prevent sync-cycles from occurring') applies to all synced attributes; sync_status_outbound gained an assignment_source parameter but no caller in this diff ever passes one, so status/comment sync loops remain unguarded. A bidirectional status sync between two systems (or the same system round-tripping) still loops exactly as before — the review-accepted goal of cycle prevention is only realized for the assignee attribute, silently narrowing the objective.

[BUG] `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` passes a new keyword to concrete integration implementations (Jira, GitHub, etc.) whose overrides do not declare `assignment_source`, raising TypeError at task runtime. For any integration whose sync_assignee_outbound override lacks the new parameter (the diff changes only the abstract method, not any concrete subclass), every outbound assignee sync task fails with TypeError instead of syncing, breaking assignee propagation for all integrations that haven't been updated in lockstep — a rolling-deploy/implementation skew the diff never addresses.

[ADVISORY] The `queued` field has no reader anywhere in the diff — it is written, serialized, and tested (test_to_dict asserts it is not None) but never consumed, making it a ships-inert feature. Operators and future readers assume timestamping semantics are enforced and load-bearing; the shared-import-time default (a real bug) went unnoticed precisely because nothing reads the value — dead field invites drift between what is recorded and what is used.

[ADVISORY] from_dict catches (ValueError, TypeError) and returns None, silently converting a malformed/poisoned queue payload into 'no source', which disables the cycle guard rather than failing loudly. If a producer ever changes the payload shape (e.g. datetime becomes a string), every downstream task treats the source as None and the sync-cycle protection silently stops applying — a degradation invisible in logs, bitten by anyone debugging why loops reappear.

[ADVISORY] IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync and IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync gained an optional parameter that existing in-tree/out-of-tree subclass overrides (which override `should_sync(self, attribute)`) will not accept once callers start passing sync_source positionally or by keyword. Third-party/custom integration subclasses that override should_sync(self, attribute) crash with TypeError as soon as any caller passes the new argument; the base-class signature change is a silent public-surface change with no call-site migration or deprecation path in this diff.

[ADVISORY] AssignmentSource.from_dict accepts an unauthenticated dict deserialized from the Celery task payload and uses its integration_id as a trusted sync-suppression control. Anything that can enqueue sync_assignee_outbound with a crafted assignment_source_dict ({"integration_id": <target integration id>, "source_name": "x"}) flips should_sync to False for that integration, silently suppressing outbound assignee/status sync for arbitrary issues — the loop-prevention check treats queue-carried data as a verified identity rather than re-deriving it from the integration record on the worker side.

[BUG] AssignmentSource.to_dict() serializes the `queued` datetime into the dict that sync_group_assignee_outbound passes as a Celery task kwarg (`assignment_source_dict`), and Celery's default JSON serializer cannot serialize a datetime, so any inbound-sync-triggered outbound assignment crashes at enqueue time. sync_group_assignee_inbound builds AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration) and passes it through GroupAssignee.assign/deassign to sync_group_assignee_outbound (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:137-143), which puts assignment_source.to_dict() (containing `queued: datetime`) into apply_async kwargs; the task publish raises a serialization error before the task runs, so inbound integrator-driven unassign/assign silently fails to propagate outbound (or raises in the caller).

[BUG] `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a class-attribute default evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource created via from_integration (which omits `queued`) carries the same import-time timestamp instead of the actual queue time. Any consumer relying on `queued` to measure assignment propagation latency gets a bogus timestamp equal to process start time, not the time the assignment was made; the field is written into every task payload with a stale value.

[ADVISORY] test_to_dict asserts `result.get("queued") is not None` — an existence-only assertion that passes for any non-None value, including the import-time-stale timestamp from the dataclass default; the to_dict/from_dict round-trip that production actually exercises (dict through Celery kwargs back into AssignmentSource) is never tested. A regression that corrupts `queued` (wrong type, stale value, or a from_dict that cannot round-trip the datetime) passes this suite; the test gives false confidence about the only field whose real production path is task-kwarg serialization.

[ADVISORY] test_from_dict_empty_array passes an empty dict, not an empty array as its name claims, so the named case (a JSON array arriving over the wire, which would raise TypeError from **-unpacking differently) is untested while the test name advertises coverage. The misnamed test masks that the list-shaped payload case is untested; a future refactor of from_dict that handles dict-shaped bad input but not list-shaped input passes the suite despite the test name promising otherwise.

[ADVISORY] The only new-branch test covers the suppression case (source integration == target integration); the comment's promised positive behavior — 'should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward', i.e. should_sync returning True when sync_source.integration_id differs from org_integration.integration_id — has no test (checked tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py and tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py; no test constructs a sync_source from a different integration and asserts outbound sync still fires). A regression that flips the comparison (e.g. `!=`, or suppressing when sync_source is set at all) still passes every test in this diff, silently breaking cross-integration assignment propagation — exactly the failure mode the cycle-prevention feature is most likely to introduce.

[ADVISORY] The matching-source test runs under self.tasks() (eager execution), which skips Celery's kwargs serialization, so the test cannot observe that assignment_source.to_dict() containing a datetime object is unserializable on the real (non-eager) publish path. The test asserts mock_sync_assignee_outbound.assert_not_called() against the eager in-process path, hiding the production enqueue-time serialization failure; in production the task never even reaches should_sync, so the cycle-prevention logic being 'tested' is not the code that actually executes first.

[ADVISORY] sync_status_outbound's abstract signature gains a required-keyword `assignment_source` parameter with no corresponding test change anywhere in the diff, and no caller in the diff passes it. Every concrete integration implementation must now accept a parameter that no test or call site in this diff exercises; implementers copying from the old signature will fail at call time if any future caller passes assignment_source, and nothing in the suite detects a mismatched override.

[BUG] AssignmentSource.to_dict() emits a raw datetime object for 'queued', which is passed directly as a Celery task kwarg in sync_group_assignee_outbound, and Celery's default JSON serializer cannot serialize datetime. Every assignment that flows through GroupAssignee.assign/deassign with an assignment_source (i.e., every inbound sync path via sync_group_assignee_inbound) raises a kombu/json serialization error at apply_async time inside the user-facing assign() request path, so the outbound sync is never enqueued and the assignment request fails or silently drops the sync; only the assignment_source=None UI path works.

[BUG] The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import time, so every AssignmentSource instance carries the process-start timestamp rather than its actual creation time. The 'queued' field records a meaningless value (process boot time, potentially days stale in long-lived workers), so any consumer relying on it for ordering, dedup, or staleness decisions gets wrong data; today it is inert, so the field misleads future consumers rather than breaking current behavior.

[BUG] The sync_assignee_outbound task gains a new required-behavior kwarg (assignment_source_dict) that old worker processes deployed during a rolling deploy do not accept, so tasks enqueued by new web nodes fail on old workers. During a rolling deploy, any outbound-assignee task produced by the new code raises TypeError on pre-upgrade workers; depending on the queue's retry policy these tasks either error out and land on the dead-letter path or retry until new workers are up, causing delayed or permanently dropped assignee syncs during the deploy window.

[ADVISORY] from_dict silently returns None on any malformed payload, which disables the cycle-prevention guard for that sync without any log or error. If a serialized AssignmentSource is corrupted or its schema evolves (field renamed, datetime format changed making cls(**dict) raise), the guard against self-triggered sync loops is silently bypassed and the outbound sync proceeds as if no source existed, re-triggering the cross-system ping-pong the mechanism was built to prevent — with no log line to diagnose why loops reappear. Author rebuttal: 'malformed dicts should never occur'; survives because the dict crosses a Celery/queue boundary and the from_dict signature exists precisely because malformed input is anticipated.

[ADVISORY] AssignmentSource is threaded through four layers (inbound sync -> GroupAssignee.assign/deassign -> sync_group_assignee_outbound -> task kwarg dict -> from_dict) as a hand-maintained parallel representation with a to_dict/from_dict pair at the boundary. Any change to AssignmentSource's fields (as the queued-field bug already demonstrates) must be replicated across the dataclass, to_dict serialization expectations, Celery's serialization format, and from_dict's reconstruction — a schema change silently breaks the guard at the from_dict boundary, where the failure mode is the silent-None path above. A single canonical serialization (or passing primitive fields explicitly at the queue boundary) removes the drift surface.
